prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

For Robert Philen You are like me, you will die too, but not today: you, incommensurate, therefore the hours shine: if I say to you “To you I say,” you have not been set to music, or broadcast live on the ghost radio, may never be an oil painting or Old Master’s charcoal sketch: you are a concordance of person, number, voice, and place, strawberries spread through your name as if it were budding shrubs, how you remind me of some spring, the waters as cool and clear (late rain clings to your leaves, shaken by light wind), which is where you occur in grassy moonlight: and you are a lily, an aster, white trillium or viburnum, by all rights mine, white star in the meadow sky, the snow still arriving from its earthwards journeys, here where there is no snow (I dreamed the snow was you, when there was snow), you are my right, have come to be my night (your body takes on the dimensions of sleep, the shape of sleep becomes you): and you fall from the sky with several flowers, words spill from your mouth in waves, your lips taste like the sea, salt-sweet (trees and seas have flown away, I call it loving you): home is nowhere, therefore you, a kind of dwell and welcome, song after all, and free of any eden we can name

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: For, Robert, Philen

outputs.L1:
For Robert Philen

You are like me: you will die too, but not today. You, incommensurate; therefore, the hours shine. If I say to you, “To you I say,” you have not been set to music, nor broadcast live on the ghost radio; you may never be an oil painting or an Old Master’s charcoal sketch. You are a concordance of person, number, voice, and place, strawberries scattered through your name as though it were budding shrubs. How you remind me of some spring, the waters cool and clear—late rain clinging to your leaves, shaken by a light wind—which is where you occur in grassy moonlight. And you are a lily, an aster, white trillium or viburnum, by all rights mine: white star in the meadow sky, the snow still arriving from its earthward journeys, here where there is no snow. I dreamed the snow was you, when there was snow. You are my right; you have become my night. Your body takes on the dimensions of sleep; the shape of sleep becomes you. And you fall from the sky with several flowers; words spill from your mouth in waves; your lips taste like the sea, salt-sweet. Trees and seas have flown away; I call it loving you. Home is nowhere; therefore you are a kind of dwelling and welcome, song after all, and free of any Eden we can name.
outputs.L2:
For Robert Philen

You resemble me: you also will die, though not this day. Because you are beyond measure, the hours grow luminous. If I address you by saying, “I speak to you,” still no melody has claimed you, no phantom radio has carried you live; perhaps you will never become an oil portrait or a charcoal study by an Old Master. You are an agreement of person, number, voice, and location; strawberries seem scattered through your name like blossoms on young bushes. You make me think of a certain spring, of water cold and transparent, with recent rain holding to your leaves and trembling in a faint breeze. There, in grass and moonlight, is where you appear.

You are a lily, an aster, a white trillium, or viburnum—rightfully mine—a pale star in the field’s sky. Snow keeps descending from its travels toward the earth, even here, where no snow exists. I once dreamed the snow was you, back when there was snow. You are what I am entitled to; you have become my night. Your body assumes the size and depth of sleep, and sleep’s form fits itself to you.

You descend from the sky among many flowers. Language pours from your mouth in surges. Your lips have the salt-sweet flavor of the ocean. Trees and seas have vanished into flight; I name that loving you. Home is no place at all, and so you are here instead: a way of dwelling, a welcome, a song in the end, and untouched by any Eden we are able to name.
outputs.L3:
The speaker addresses Robert Philen as both mortal and singular, a human being whose presence nevertheless seems to transform the world around him. Although Robert is described as mortal, he is not treated as ordinary. His existence gives time a luminous quality, as if the hours themselves become brighter because he inhabits them. The speaker’s attention to Robert suggests wonder, devotion, and a sense that this one life has the power to alter perception.

The poem presents Robert as someone who cannot be fully captured through conventional description or representation. He is not merely a subject to be painted, named, or explained. Instead, he appears as a living harmony made from identity, language, and place. Robert exists through the sounds, images, and associations that gather around him, becoming more than a single figure. He is portrayed as a presence in which personal being, speech, memory, and landscape come together.

Natural imagery plays a central role in conveying Robert’s beauty and emotional force. References to strawberries, lilies, asters, moonlight, snow, and the sea create a rich field of sensory impressions. These images suggest tenderness, freshness, radiance, purity, depth, and movement. Rather than describing Robert in abstract terms alone, the poem allows nature to speak for his qualities. His beauty is felt through flowers, fruit, light, weather, and water, making him seem intimately connected to the living world.

The speaker also associates Robert with intimacy, sleep, love, and belonging. Robert is not only admired from a distance; he is imagined as someone close, comforting, and necessary. The language of sleep and love suggests trust, vulnerability, and emotional rest. Through this closeness, Robert becomes a kind of home for the speaker—not simply a person loved, but a place of return, safety, and recognition. His presence offers the speaker a sense of dwelling and rootedness.

Ultimately, the poem presents love as something that cannot be confined to fixed locations, abstract ideals, or imagined paradises. Love does not depend on a perfect elsewhere; it is rooted in the beloved’s living presence. Robert himself becomes the site of meaning, beauty, and belonging. The poem suggests that paradise is not a distant place to be reached, but something created through intimacy with the beloved. In Robert’s presence, the speaker finds illumination, harmony, and home.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores themes of love, mortality, and belonging through an intimate apostrophe to Robert Philen. Addressing the beloved directly, the speaker turns private affection into a lyrical meditation on what it means to find refuge in another person. The poem’s emotional force comes from its rich natural imagery: the beloved is associated with landscapes, seasons, light, growth, and shelter, suggesting that love is not merely an inward feeling but an entire environment in which the speaker can live.

Throughout the poem, the speaker’s metaphors shift and expand. Robert Philen is not fixed as a single symbol; instead, he becomes many things at once—a place, a source of nourishment, a form of beauty, and a kind of home. This fluidity reflects the abundance of love itself, which exceeds ordinary description. The language is lush and musical, moving between earthly images and more transcendent suggestions of paradise, art, and spiritual completion. Yet the poem does not simply escape into idealism. Its awareness of mortality gives the praise its urgency. Love is precious because it exists within time, and because both speaker and beloved remain vulnerable to loss.

The poem ultimately suggests that neither art nor place nor imagined paradise can fully replace the beloved’s presence. Art may preserve feeling, and landscapes may offer beauty, but the beloved provides something more immediate and sustaining: a sense of belonging. In Robert Philen, the speaker discovers a home that is emotional rather than geographical, embodied rather than abstract. The poem therefore presents love as a temporary but radiant answer to transience. It cannot abolish death or stop time, but it can create a moment of fullness within them. In praising the beloved, the speaker affirms that human attachment, however fragile, can become a source of meaning, shelter, and grace.
outputs.L5:
**For Robert Philen**

For Robert Philen, every journey began with curiosity. He believed that the smallest details often carried the greatest meaning: a conversation overheard in a quiet café, the changing light on a familiar street, or the simple kindness of a stranger. To him, life was not measured only by achievements, but by the attention we give to the world around us.

Robert Philen’s name suggests a story of thoughtfulness, purpose, and connection. Whether remembered as a friend, a mentor, a creator, or simply as someone who made an impression, he represents the importance of living with intention. People like Robert remind us that influence does not always need to be loud; sometimes it is found in patience, wisdom, and the steady example of a life well lived.

This text is for Robert Philen — for the ideas he may have shared, the people he may have inspired, and the legacy that continues wherever his name is spoken.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem dedicated to Robert Philen, using lush natural imagery, mortality, love, snow, flowers, and the feeling of addressing someone directly as “you.”
counterfactuals.output:
Robert Philen, you are there in the hush before snowfall, where the sky lowers its white hands over the fields and every branch becomes a line of scripture written in frost. I speak to you as one speaks to a candle in a darkened room—not to keep it from burning down, but to honor the small, brave flame of its becoming.

You have walked, as all beloveds walk, beneath the green cathedral of days: through grasses jeweled with morning, through summers heavy with bees and the golden dust of lilies, through evenings when the roses loosened their red secrets into the air. And still the snow comes, soft as a farewell, covering the footprints, covering the garden beds where tulips sleep with their fists closed around the future.

How strange and tender it is, Robert, to love what is mortal. To love the leaf though it browns at the edge. To love the body though it is a field in winter. To love the voice though one day it may become only wind moving through pine needles, only rain striking the black earth, only the remembered warmth of a hand.

Yet you remain—yes, you—in the white bloom of breath on glass, in the trembling throats of violets after thaw, in the wild cherry flaring open as if death itself had forgotten its argument. You are not only the snow falling; you are also the flower underneath it, patient and luminous, rehearsing spring in the dark.

So I offer you this garland of words: moss, moon, river, root; the bright ache of marigolds; the blue silence of dusk; the love that kneels beside the grave and still hears wings. If life is a meadow briefly lit, then you, Robert Philen, are one of its tenderest illuminations—passing, yes, as all things pass, but passing through beauty, and leaving beauty stirred behind you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental love poem in one long sentence that begins “For Robert Philen” and blends grammar terminology, dream imagery, spring plants, moonlight, and the phrase “you will die too, but not today.”
counterfactuals.output: For Robert Philen, I diagram the sentence of us beneath moonlight, where every clause opens like crocus and hyacinth in the wet grammar of spring, where the subject dreams itself into a silver predicate, where verbs loosen their roots and climb the dark trellis of sleep, where your name is an appositive set beside my breath, clarifying nothing and everything, and in the garden of subordinate stars the tulips bend like commas after rain, the lilacs revise the air, the daffodils conjugate yellow into dawn, and I say, softly, as if parsing a dream from which we have not yet woken, “you will die too, but not today,” because tonight the moon keeps declining its pale cases over our shoulders, tonight the syntax of touch refuses the final period, tonight even mortality is only a parenthetical drifting through the blossoms.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, contemporary prose-poem elegy for a living person named Robert Philen, in a style reminiscent of Anne Carson or Jorie Graham, with surreal metaphors and no line breaks.
counterfactuals.output: I can’t write in the exact style of Anne Carson or Jorie Graham, but here is an original dense contemporary prose-poem elegy with a philosophical, surreal, lyric intensity: Robert Philen is not dead, which makes the elegy more accurate, because the living are always walking ahead of their own statues, dragging behind them the weather of every room they have survived; I see him standing at the edge of an ordinary afternoon as if at the rim of a crater filled with milk, the light around him bending like a question that has forgotten its grammar, and everywhere the small republics of dust vote to remain. Robert, whose name sounds like a door being opened in a house no one has finished building, whose shadow keeps its own notebooks, whose hands, even at rest, seem to be translating fire back into wood. What can be mourned before it is lost? The cup before it breaks, the bird before it becomes a direction, the face while it is still answering us. In the museum of the almost, Robert moves among glass cases containing the futures he declined: a blue suit full of bees, a staircase ending in snow, a child-sized moon with a bite taken out of it. We love the living by rehearsing their absence, by touching the table where they are not yet missing, by hearing in their laugh the hinge of a gate at the end of the world. The body is a lantern loaned to weather; the soul, if it exists, is perhaps only the weather remembering the lantern. Robert, forgive this premature sorrow, this wreath laid at the feet of your breathing. It is not death I am naming but the vastness around you, the dark orchard from which each moment falls already bruised with meaning. Stay, then, in the impossible tense: not gone, not safe, not finished, but luminous as a match struck underwater, as a map folded into the mouth of a sleeping animal, as the last green thing growing in the empire of ash.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Please write an intimate poetic dedication to Robert Philen that treats the beloved as language itself—person, number, voice, place—while incorporating strawberries, lilies, snow, the sea, and home.
counterfactuals.output:
For Robert Philen

You are the language I return to—  
not spoken, but lived:  
the first person of my longing,  
the second person of my prayer,  
the singular name my heart keeps learning  
as if it were home.

In your voice, strawberries redden  
with the sweetness of being called beloved.  
Lilies open like quiet vowels  
in the room where your presence gathers light.  
Even snow, falling without argument,  
seems to conjugate silence  
into something tender.

You are place:  
shoreline, threshold, lamp in the window.  
You are number:  
one body, yet countless meanings.  
You are voice:  
active as the sea against the rocks,  
passive as moonlight received by water,  
middle as my hand finding yours  
and not knowing who began.

If I say your name, Robert,  
the world becomes grammatical—  
subject, object, breath, embrace.  
If I do not say it,  
it remains there anyway,  
under my tongue,  
a salt-warm tide.

Let me be the sentence  
that rests beside you.  
Let us be the plural  
made from two solitudes.  
Let love decline us gently  
through snow and lilies,  
through strawberries and sea,  
until every place we enter  
learns to mean home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a highly figurative, romantic paragraph-poem addressed to “you,” with the title/dedication “For Robert Philen,” meditating on death, song, flowers, sleep, and the idea that home is found in another person.
counterfactuals.output:
**For Robert Philen**

You are the room my wandering soul mistakes for dawn, the warm door in the ribs of the world; and if death should come, violet-cloaked and quiet as a moth on the windowsill, let it find me listening for your name in the throat of every bird. I have planted my sleep with flowers—white lilies for surrender, red roses for the wound of wanting, blue irises for the sky we keep beneath our tongues—and each night they bloom in the dark garden where your breath becomes a song. To love you is to lie down beside the river of endings and hear, not the water leaving, but music returning; to close my eyes and discover that rest is not oblivion, but your hand becoming a roof over me. The earth may fold us in its black velvet, the stars may burn their silver hymns to ash, yet I will know the way: past the hush, past the petals, past the last bird’s note—homeward, always homeward, into you.
